newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels threaten to kill embassy hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels threaten to kill embassy hostages.

text.p: Leftist guerrillas threatened to kill up to 490 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Wednesday as hopes faded of a quick breakthrough a day after the building was stormed.

The rebels called on President Alberto Fujimori to personally negotiate for the release of the captives, including two Peruvian ministers and at least 15 ambassadors from Asia, Europe and the Americas.
The Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels said they would kill the hostages unless the government freed up to 500 jailed comrades.
"If they do not release our prisoners, we will all die in here," one guerrilla told a local radio station from inside the embassy residence.
Tensions rose dramatically around midday (1700 GMT) when the rebels threatened to kill hostages, starting with Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, within an hour unless Fujimori joined negotiations.
But the deadline passed apparently without bloodshed and the guerrillas released four elderly hostages.
Earlier an unexplained explosion and gunfire rocked the building.
The rebels said they would free no more captives until they received medicine for injured hostages and rebels.

While estimates by the government and released hostages put the number of captives between 200 and 300, a letter signed by the captives, including Tudela, and faxed to relatives said the rebels were holding 490 men.
Speaking to local media from inside the building, the rebels accused the government of intransigence. They said they had booby trapped the entrances to the residence.

"Up to now, there is an intransigent position (from the authorities). The only solution is a political one," MRTA member Walter Loayza said, adding that the rebels wanted transport for them and freed comrades to a guerrilla-controlled jungle area.
Fujimori, who suspended all public activities and called an emergency cabinet meeting for Thursday morning, has so far not commented publicly on the attack.
However, in a conversation with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, the president said Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila was handling negotiations.
Guerrilla spokesmen said they had targeted the Japanese ambassador's home in protest at Tokyo's support for President Alberto Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, and his economic policies.
Japan was chosen as a target "due to the constant meddling of the Japanese government in Peru," one rebel spokesman said.
Governments around the world urged Peru to do everything in its power to protect the hostages and not use force to flush out the rebels.

Japan, Germany, Austria, Spain, Greece, South Korea, Panama, Malaysia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Brazil, Cuba, Guatemala, Honduras and Canada confirmed their ambassadors were among the hostages. The United States ambassador was present at the reception but left before the attack, according to the State Department.

The drama began around 8 p.m local time (0100 GMT) Tuesday when heavily-armed rebels attacked the building, firing a rocket from outside, and around 20 rebels swarmed inside after blowing a hole in an outside wall, according to witnesses.
Some unconfirmed reports said guerrillas disguised as waiters joined the attack from the inside.
Juan Carlos Mejia, head of the special police task force handling the siege, confirmed that the rebels had smuggled in ammunition among flowers and Christmas cake.
After an initial chaotic shootout with police and security guards, there was calm for several hours while about 80 women and old people were gradually released.
One of those freed, foreign correspondents' association president Sally Bowen, said the guerrillas -- dressed in black and armed with machine-guns and grenades -- were "pretty calm and determined."
But "it was scary, especially during the shooting at the beginning," she said.
As well as Tudela, the Peruvian hostages included Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante Sanguineti, Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja and at least three local legislators.
The rebels said they had 400 to 500 comrades in jail and their top priority was the release of their leader Victor Polay, who was imprisoned in 1992.
The attack was a major blow to Fujimori's government, which had claimed virtual victory in a 16-year war with communist rebels of the MRTA and the larger and better-known Maoist Shining Path.

The succesful campaign against guerrillas has been a major factor in the return of economic stability and foreign investment. In an immediate sign of the impact of the attack, the Lima stock market suspended trading in mid-session after heavy falls.
